content.thinking:
I'm weighing whether to use relative imports given this repo's existing samples pattern, since the harness bundles files with relative paths and the prior treasureHoard version follows that convention too.

Since I can't test anything, I need to be careful and deliberate here. I'm designing a League of Legends-style treasure hoard: a hextech-themed open chest with hinged lid, overflowing gold coins, glowing gem clusters, a crown, tipped goblets, and loose gems, roughly 2m wide and 1.1m tall overall. I'm setting up a root joint plus a hinge joint for the lid so it can be posed open, keeping track of how parts built after a pose will land in that new position.

I'm working out the rotation math so the lid swings up and back correctly around the hinge's X axis, solving for the right angle and coordinates so the open lid looks physically correct relative to the chest body.

Now I'm positioning the chest itself near the back of the hoard scene, defining its footprint, depth, and body height so the pile of treasure can spill forward and sideways in front of it.

Sizing the chest more like a stylized chunky treasure box, I'm working out the body dimensions and hinge placement, then shaping the lid as a half-cylinder arch extruded along the x-axis to form the classic domed chest top.

Working out the rotation math to confirm which half of the cylinder ends up facing upward after transforming coordinates — rather than trust the Euler angle juggling, I decide to just verify directly which local axis maps to world up.

Working through the basis further, local x maps to world +Z, so the half-cylinder only covers the front, needing a thetaStart/thetaLength adjustment to get the top half right. Given the risk of subtle error, I decide instead to use an explicit rotation option, applying a 90-degree Euler Z rotation in model space.

Defining lid outline...

For the chest body itself, I'm planning a wood-painted box with grain running along x, plus corner posts and iron/gold bands for decoration.

For the open interior, I want a coin mound bulging above the rim instead of a flat floor — the body top sits around 0.45 with a gold heap mesh rising over the edge, framed by rim trim boxes. Coins themselves get modeled as small merged cylinders (~250 instances grouped by color to keep part count low), positioned across an analytic heightfield representing the mound surface rather than raw mesh collision.

I'm defining the pile as a few overlapping ellipsoid mounds with their own position and size parameters, giving each a flat-shaded gold material with mottled coloring, then scattering coins across each mound's surface by sampling random points within its ellipse and orienting them to the local surface normal with slight random tilt so they look embedded and tumbled. I'll merge the coins into a few geometries by color (gold, light gold, dark gold, silver) using mergeGeometries with per-instance transform matrices applied to cloned geometry, importing that utility from three/addons as shown in the docs, and I'm double-checking that all the cylinder geometries share consistent indexed attributes so the merge works cleanly.

For a few standout coins, I'm considering giving them a visible decorative face using a small circular texture with a hex-star emblem rather than plain geometry, since a handful of "hero coins" propped on edge could use that extra visual detail economically. I'm sketching out a short list of textures to create — the coin emblem, a hextech sigil for the chest's front lock plate, a filigree trim strip, sparkle glints near the gems, and a patterned velvet cloth texture to drape under the treasure pile.

I'm weighing where to add a crown crest texture and whether the goblet's engraved band can be handled with procedural paint bands by height and angle on the lathe geometry instead of a texture, which would be more efficient. For the overall material style I'm leaning into a painterly, hand-painted look — rich gold with orange-toned shadows, pale yellow highlights, and strong rim lighting with some teal-purple magic accents, built through custom paint functions rather than texture maps, while gems get faceted low-poly geometry with a glow effect and crystal spike clusters for extra sparkle.

Now I'm sketching out the crown itself: a lathe-based tapered band sitting on the coin pile, topped with eight gem-studded points, arching bands meeting at a central orb/finial, and a dark red velvet cap peeking through the top, aiming for a tall, angular Demacian-style silhouette.

I'm working out how to position and tilt the crown using a transform helper that combines position, rotation, and scale into a matrix so each sub-part can be placed and oriented consistently relative to the whole assembly.

I'll apply the xf helper to position the crown and goblets too. For the goblets, I'm planning three: two standing upright (one tall by the chest, one in front) and one tipped over spilling coins and gems, so I need to work out the lathe profile for the goblet shape.

Working out the goblet profile points...

I'm thinking some goblets could hold a mounded pile of coins or glowing gems peeking above the rim, varying the fill between hextech blue wine and treasure. For the lathe outline, I need to make sure the point order is consistent so the loop closes cleanly.

I'll keep segment counts low (around 10) for a faceted look rather than smooth, and avoid smoothing on thin-walled shapes to prevent self-intersection errors — relying on carefully placed sharp points instead. For the chest ornament I'm planning gold decorative bands.

Adding vertical body bands as proud boxes, a horizontal gold trim strip, and base feet blocks, then settling on a deep blue-teal and gold hextech color scheme with a cyan glow for the chest.

Coin piles will sit directly on the ground plane rather than a floor slab, built as flattened dome mounds using partial sphere geometry restricted to the upper hemisphere so their bases sit flush at y=0 without sinking below the surface.

For each mound I'm defining a height field based on a scaled hemisphere function, then placing coins slightly embedded into this surface so they look naturally piled rather than floating -- using enough geometry segments to keep the surface smooth and adjusting coin positions by small offsets to avoid gaps or overlap with the analytic mound shape.

Coin orientation comes from the ellipsoid's surface normal at each point, tilted randomly up to 35 degrees for most coins and up to 60 degrees for a quarter of them so some sit more on edge, giving a messier hoard look rather than uniform scales.

I'm working out triangle budget for the coin count -- cutting cylinder sides from 10 to 8 per coin brings triangle cost down to around 14k for roughly 450 coins, leaving enough budget for the rest of the scene.

For coloring, I'll use three or four flat gold tones plus maybe a hint of silver, applying position-based noise paint across the merged geometry so coins get some natural variation without per-vertex overhead -- flat shading with lighting should still give a nice faceted look.

For the hero coins, I'm planning around ten larger ones (r 0.07) standing on edge against the mounds, built from a thin cylinder body plus two circular face planes slightly offset so a textured coin-emblem decal can sit on front and back, each oriented along the surface normal with the back face flipped to face the opposite direction.

For the emblem decal itself, I'm designing a small SVG with rim rings, a six-point star motif, a center gem, and beaded trim in warm gold tones with darker strokes and pale highlights for depth.

Now I'm working out individual cut gems using a lathe geometry to approximate a faceted diamond shape, defining crown and pavilion profile points to get that brilliant-cut silhouette.

I'm assigning distinct colors per gem type -- ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, and a cyan hextech crystal -- and tuning glow strength so most gems keep visible faceting (around 0.5 emissive) while the hextech crystal and rune glyph glow at full intensity for a more magical effect.

For the crystal clusters, I'm building hexagonal prisms with pointed tops using a 6-segment lathe profile that tapers to a point, tilted via an axis direction, then arranging a couple of clusters (starting with amethyst) using this shape.

For loose gems, I'm scattering around 16 small cut gems across the mounds with varied tilt and glow, plus adding flat sparkle cards with star-glint textures standing upright at a slight lean to catch light.

For the goblets, I'm detailing them with a ring of jeweled studs and engraving bands onto the lathed surface using a custom paint function based on height and angle.

For the chest, I'm designing a front lock plate as a gold hexagonal shield with a keyhole and cyan gem, plus a glowing hextech glyph strip inlaid into the wooden front board.

Now I'm adding a lid underside lining with a quilted crimson pattern using a thin extruded slab and a diamond pattern generated from sine functions for the tufted look.

For the chest interior, I'm keeping the body solid but adding a dome-shaped coin mound inside that bulges above the rim and spills over the front edge, cascading onto a larger mound outside the chest.

I need to allow mounds with a vertical center offset, since a hemisphere floating with its base plane raised could expose a hollow underside where it overhangs the chest. I'm checking whether mound E's base disc at y=0.3 stays hidden inside the chest body or whether its front overhang beyond z=0.3 would reveal an open bottom — but it seems the front mound should cover that gap.

Working through the geometry, if I set mound E's center at y=0.2, its base sits below the front mound's surface height at that depth, so it stays hidden. I'm now defining the full mound list with centers, radii, and heights, sketching an overall footprint roughly 2.2 wide and 1.5 deep to lay out the composition.

Now I'm placing the remaining pieces: a chest at the back center, crystal clusters behind on left and right, a crown resting on the front-right mound, upright goblets on the front-left and right sides plus a tipped one at front center, and several additional mounds (ML, MR, and smaller front-left/front-right bumps) to round out the terrain around the chest.

I'm also working out neat coin stacks—3-10 coin columns with slight random rotation—sampled onto flat spots on the mounds, with their bases sunk slightly into the heightfield surface so they look naturally settled rather than floating.

For extra treasure variety, I'm adding a gem-studded goblet and considering a small stack of gold ingot bars (trapezoid-shaped frustums) arranged pyramid-style on the left side to break up the silhouette, using a rotated low-segment cylinder trick to fake the frustum box shape.

Writing ingot extrude code...

I'll also refine the chest with raised stud details along its metal bands and a lock plate for added realism.

For the latch, I'm figuring out placement: the lock plate with keyhole texture goes on the body front, with a matching latch tongue on the lid's front edge that lines up with it when closed. I need to work out the lid's geometry carefully since it's a half-cylinder arch extruded along x, meaning its curved surface and front-facing edge shift position depending on whether it's open or closed.

I'm checking whether the arch's solid extrusion needs hollowing, or if a slightly inset lining slab is enough to reveal the crimson underside. Tracking how the bottom face's normal rotates when the lid swings open 105°, so the lining ends up visibly facing the camera rather than hidden.

I'll offset the lining slab so it protrudes only 3mm beyond the lid's bottom face, avoiding z-fighting while keeping most of it embedded—then build the quilted panel as a simple box geometry.

For the quilted texture, I'm painting a diamond pattern on the lining based on position rather than UVs, with darker gold borders near the edges to form a piped rim. For the chest body's front face, I plan to paint horizontal wood planks keyed to vertical position plus grain noise for texture.

For the lid's arched surface, I need to rethink the plank orientation since it curves—rather than straight horizontal seams, I'll compute angle bands around the hinge axis so the planks follow the arc, and handle the end faces separately since their seams would radiate like pie slices.

Now I'm sketching out the chest's structural dimensions: a plinth with gold-capped feet, and a body box sized roughly 1.1 x 0.45 x 0.7, positioning the feet and body vertically so the mound hides the lower portion.

Still writing chest geometry...

Checking the overlap math, I realize the front mound is covering too much of the chest area, burying the lock plate and runes I wanted visible. I need to redesign the coin spill to be a smaller, off-center pour instead of one large central mound so the front detailing stays visible.

I realize the flat-dome approach would just look like a solid tabletop rather than an open chest, so instead I'll construct the chest body as a hollow box—floor plus four walls—with the interior lined in red so the coin mound actually reads as sitting inside an open container.

I'm leaving a gap near the rim where dark crimson interior shows through above the mound's narrowing hemisphere. I'll make the walls wood on the outside with a thin crimson velvet lining proud on the inside, keeping the part count manageable, and now I'm working out how coins should be placed on the mound so they stay visible above the rim without being swallowed by the wall height.

For coin placement I'm sampling random points within each mound's elliptical footprint, filtering out ones too low (y below ~0.4) so they don't get buried, then computing the surface height and tilting each coin's orientation slightly with a small offset below the normal. I'm worried about coins placed near the mound's base where the radius approaches its max — their tilt and thickness could make them dip slightly below the floor, which might exceed my allowed tolerance.

So I'm writing a clamp function: it figures out the lowest point of each coin given its radius, thickness, and tilt angle relative to vertical, and if that extent would go below zero it raises the coin's center just enough to keep it flush with or above the floor. I also want each crystal cluster to sit on a small dark rock-like base rather than floating directly on the floor, so I'll add a flattened boulder shape beneath each cluster painted in a cool, dark tone.

I'm scattering a few loose coins near the edges of the mounds, flat on the floor with slight random tilts to look naturally spilled, while skipping any leaning coins for simplicity. For goblet placement, I'll bury their bases slightly into the terrain height at each position, and for the tipped goblet I'm working out a tilted transform so it rests on its side atop a coin heap, with a trail of spilled coins and gems extending outward from its mouth along the tilt direction, following the terrain height.

I'm defining helper functions for the mound height field and its surface normal via finite differences, then using those to scatter coins naturally across regions where the terrain rises above a threshold, weighting placement toward the mound areas.

Still refining coin placement...

Confirming the interior pile top sits at the I mound's max height, well above E's lower top, so rejection sampling correctly isolates the right region at trivial cost. Now I'm setting up each mound's mesh using a half-sphere geometry for the base shape.

For texture, I'll paint the mound surface with a mottled gold-brown scale pattern using varied gold tones with dark edges — this gives even the bare mound a coin-pile look before placing real coins on top, so gaps between coins still read as part of the hoard. I'm aiming for roughly 420 coins total.

Now I'm working out the crown geometry — defining a lathed profile with outer and inner radius points at different heights to create the band shape, closing the polygon into a crown silhouette about 0.34 tall and 0.19 in radius.

Placing gem geometry around the band...

Positioning each spire around the band at radius 0.2 with outward-facing extrusion, alternating tall and short gothic points for a crown-like silhouette, and adding small glowing gems partway up plus pearl tips. I'm also sketching four catmull-rom arches rising from the band to meet at a central apex above.

Since there's only one real joint besides the lid, I need to be careful that nearby parts don't accidentally bind to the lid joint instead of root -- I'll explicitly pass bone: root to every sweep, extrude, and lathe call except where lid attachment is intended, wrapping creation in helper functions to enforce this. Finally I'm placing a gold orb at the apex along with a hextech-style crystal accent.

Now I'm designing the velvet cap as a crimson dome sitting atop the band, with an ermine fur trim rendered as a flattened torus painted with cream and dark speckles for the classic royal look, then positioning the whole crown with a slight tilt on the head.

I'm adjusting the crown's seat height so it sinks slightly into the surrounding coin pile, scaling it up to 1.15 for a chunkier, more prominent look, and placing it on a flattened mound at a specific hoard location. Now I'm sketching out a goblet-building function that constructs the cup body as a lathe shape with rim gems, a stem knob, and a base ring.

Working out goblet profile points...

Adding glowing liquid fill...

Writing lathe shader logic...

Rather than handle the tilted goblet case geometrically, I'll just pass an axis vector parameter into the paint function so it can decide which wall is outer using the dot product with that axis, falling back to a gold base paint with a banded pattern for the decoration.

For the gold itself I'm blending shadow, mid, and highlight tones based on light direction with some noise, plus a cooler purple-brown bounce light for the underside. Then I'm planning similar warm-to-cool treatments for wood grain with plank seams and a crimson velvet quilt with diamond seam stitching.

I'm also designing a hand-painted cel-shading style for stone and gold surfaces, quantizing the lighting into three bands (shadow/mid/highlight) with noise-perturbed thresholds so the edges look like painterly splotches rather than flat digital gradients.

For the scene layout, I'm placing two crystal clusters — one cyan/sapphire hextech group on the left-back, one amethyst/ruby group on the right — growing out from rock mounds built with flat-shaded hemispheres surrounded by smaller boulder shapes, with each crystal's lathe profile and outward-leaning orientation positioned relative to the rock's surface.

Refining the crystal lathe to end in a six-faceted pointed tip with a subtle shoulder bevel for a more gem-like silhouette, keeping segment count low so flat shading reveals distinct facets under the glow lighting. I'm also designing a sparkle texture as a four-point star with a soft white-yellow glow for the crystal highlights before moving on to the card frame details.

Now I'm placing sparkle cards using frame positions near each gem plus a few above the crown, with sizes varying slightly for a natural scattered look, and standing each card upright by nudging its anchor point down to account for the card's base. For textures, I'm planning a coin-like hextech star emblem and a lock plate with a hex shield and keyhole, making sure only the gem portion glows rather than the whole plate.

I'm also sketching a runes strip texture with glowing cyan glyphs on a transparent background so only the strokes remain visible when overlaid proud of the wood surface, plus a sparkle texture and a crest/medallion emblem (shield with wings) to decorate the crown band front and possibly the lid's top center as an inlaid round medallion, oriented to match the lid's curved surface when open.

Now I'm working out the lid arch geometry so the medallion sits flush: I want to raise a small gold disc on the arch's top and ensure the polygon facets include a flat horizontal edge at the very top, which means choosing an even number of segments so no single vertex lands exactly at the peak, giving two symmetric vertices and a flat top edge instead.

I'm also considering decorative extras like a rolled parchment map or a treasure-map card, but deciding these add unnecessary risk and complexity — I'll skip them and stick to the core texture set: coin, lock plate, runes, sparkle, crest, and maybe a goblet motif.

Settling on five textures - COIN, LOCK, RUNES, SPARK, CREST - skipping extras like engrave bands or banners to keep the prop count lean, with CREST doing double duty as the crown's front plaque.

Now I'm estimating part counts: merging coins into groups and studs together, but keeping gems and crystals as separate parts since each needs its own glow. That lands me around 150-250 total parts, with roughly 12 individual crystals and 24 loose gem pieces contributing most of that count.

Tallying up the rest - chests, crowns, goblets, mounds, coins, gems, stacks, sparkles, rocks - pushes the total to about 250 parts. Since I can't test the code directly, I need to write it carefully with strict typing in mind, making sure every import is actually used. I'm setting up imports for THREE.js geometry merging utilities, the builder and frame helpers, math and path utilities, paint/texture functions, and the glow kit - and I should check other sample files to confirm the merge geometries import path resolves correctly.
